source.title: Forget What Comes Next: LLM Unlearning via Statistical Independence
source.authors: Andrii Shkabrii; Claudia Plant; Martin Pawelczyk

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It evaluates whether forgotten information remains recoverable with a linear probe of hidden states, a different internal-access test from the attacks named in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper tests hidden-state extraction with a linear probe trained on retain data and reports PINT's result relative to other unlearning methods. It does not test recovery by fine-tuning, activation-direction ablation, quantization, or prompting. The WMDP-Cyber and MMLU results measure PINT's forgetting and utility, not recovery attacks.
record.test_reason: Mainly a new-method paper (PINT). Its one recovery-style test is a retain-trained linear probe that extracts forgotten TOFU tokens from hidden states, compared across PINT and six baselines (Fig. 7). This bears on C (access blocked rather than deleted) and F (a newer method resisting internal extraction). It is a different method from the originals' attacks. No fine-tuning, ablation, quantization or prompting attack is run.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. PINT gives the best average forgetting-utility trade-off across eight settings (mean area 0.95 vs at most 0.90). It is the only method making Gaussian poisons undetectable with most utility kept, and it scales to 70B. A linear probe recovers fewer forgotten tokens from PINT's hidden states than from the baselines'. The authors caution that passing current benchmarks does not prove information is unrecoverable.
record.recipe_differences: PINT is a new HSIC-based unlearning objective, rather than a recovery attack or a direct replication of the methods named in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The linear probe is evaluated at each method's most accurate layer. The paper reports that the best layer varies by method; it does not state a layer-specific probe comparison in the text.

fits_no_version.finding: On Gaussian poisons (OLMo-2 2.7B), baseline unlearning methods leave poisons statistically detectable at acceptable utility. PINT makes them undetectable while keeping 91% utility, against at most 63% for the others.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearning methods leave a statistically detectable gradient trace of the forgotten training examples (residual memorization), measured by poison detectability.

fits_no_version.finding: On bioS, RMU forgets the occupation but also the retained major attribute of the same people (99% to 19%). PINT keeps the major at 97%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Representation-collapse unlearning (RMU) damages closely related retained knowledge.

record.problems: The internal-recovery evidence is a linear probe, not fine-tuning or activation ablation. Its probe accuracy is plotted rather than given as a method-specific number in the text. The authors note that benchmark metrics are imperfect proxies and that passing them does not prove information can never be recovered.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 6 reports many Pareto-frontier settings across eight benchmarks and methods; individual plotted settings are not separately recorded here. They measure forgetting and utility, not recovery attacks. The explicit 70B results and the hidden-state probe result are retained.

untested.parts: Whether simple attacks recover knowledge from PINT, other than the TOFU linear probe; general ability at 70B beyond MMLU.
Not tested: no relearning or fine-tuning attack.
No activation-direction ablation. The probe values per method are not readable, so it is unknown whether baselines retain probe-extractable knowledge above chance.
Not tested. bioS uses held-out paraphrases only as the evaluation format, not as an attack on a separately unlearned model.
PINT's resistance to fine-tuning, ablation, quantization and prompting attacks is not tested. The probe gives only a relative ranking.

missing.what: Per-method linear-probe next-token accuracy on the TOFU 10% forget set, with best layer and seed range, plus any pre-unlearning or chance reference.
MUSE News: every method loses at least a third of its utility before matching retrain-level KnowMem forgetting. This is a utility cost relevant to A.
bioS: RMU's retained-attribute accuracy drops from 0.99 to 0.19, while PINT's stays at 0.97.

record.verdict_notes: This is a method paper. Its rows R1/R2 are PINT's own results, so the A verdict covers only forgetting with utility kept, not robustness to attack. The reader's C 'supports' label is unfounded: the text gives no absolute probe accuracies or reference level, only that PINT ranks lowest. No C or F verdict is given until Fig. 7 values are extracted. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Only a linear-probe extraction test is used as an attack; fine-tuning, activation ablation, quantization, and prompting attacks are not tested.
Recovery by fine-tuning on unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten examples is not tested.
The study tests linear-probe extraction from hidden states, not activation-direction ablation or causal access-blocking directly.
Recovery by quantization is not tested.
Recovery by rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information is not tested.
PINT is evaluated with a linear probe, but the study does not test its resistance to the attacks listed in versions B, C's ablation alternative, D, or E.

rows.subject: Llama-3-70B
rows.operation_detail: PINT unlearning of hazardous cybersecurity knowledge
rows.note: PINT brings accuracy close to the stated random-guessing target.
rows.check: Version id 'V1' is invalid; use A. This row is the study's own method's forgetting result, not a recovery attack. WMDP-Cyber falls from 0.530 to 0.276 against a 0.250 chance level.

rows.operation_detail: PINT unlearning of hazardous cybersecurity knowledge
rows.note: The authors describe this as a drop of only 0.2 points.
rows.check: Version id 'V1' is invalid; use A. This is PINT's own utility result: MMLU 0.752 before, 0.750 after.

rows.subject: Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Train a linear probe on retain-set data to predict next tokens from hidden states; report the probe's highest accuracy over layers on the forget set
rows.measure: Next-token accuracy from hidden state on forgotten tokens
rows.baseline: Random guess 0.125; other unlearning methods have higher probe accuracy than PINT, according to the text
rows.uncertainty: Range over three seeds (error bars); numerical range not stated in text
rows.note: The text says the probe recovers fewer forgotten tokens from PINT's hidden states than from any other tested method. The plotted value is not assigned here because the figure's flattened labels do not make a precise method-value mapping reliable.
rows.check: Version ids V1/V3 are invalid. The baseline is wrong: 0.125 random guess belongs to bioS (Fig. 8), not Fig. 7. Fig. 7 gives no pre-unlearning or chance probe level. Per-method probe accuracies are figure-only and not readable here, so absolute recoverability cannot be judged. Only the ordering is stated: PINT is lowest.

relation.reason: Its own WMDP-Cyber/MMLU results bear on the forgetting-with-utility part of A. The retain-trained TOFU linear probe bears weakly on C and F.

tranche.reason: PINT is a new HSIC-based unlearning method aimed at the same question: forgetting targeted knowledge while keeping utility.

source_check.notes: The 70B result covers WMDP-Cyber only (three seeds, no Bio). On WMDP, PINT and RMU update only the MLP output projections of layers 5-7. Zephyr-7B WMDP results appear only as Figure 6 frontiers. No recovery attack is run on any WMDP checkpoint. The only recovery-style test is a retain-trained linear probe on TOFU 10% (Fig. 7).
